text.note: See the Greek deck, card 7 and card 21.
Greek ἐν takes the dative only, as in ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ, in the land. Motion to a place is εἰς with the accusative, as in εἰς τὴν χώρᾱν. See also the Greek deck, card 7.

li1.note: Where Latin uses the ablative absolute, Greek uses the genitive absolute: a noun and a participle, both in the genitive, outside the main construction, as in τοῦ βασιλέως λῡ́οντος, “while the king looses.”

li3.note: After a primary tense, Greek keeps the mood of the direct question. After a secondary tense, the optative may be used instead.

sa1.note: After a verb of striving, Greek usually takes ὅπως with the future indicative, and the negative is μή. ὅπως with the subjunctive is less common.

ta3.note: Where Latin uses the ablative absolute, Greek uses the genitive absolute: a noun and a participle, both in the genitive, outside the main construction, as in τοῦ βασιλέως λῡ́οντος, “while the king looses.”

au2.note: Greek purpose is introduced by ἵνα, ὅπως, or ὡς, and the negative is μή. The subjunctive follows a primary tense, and the optative may follow a secondary tense.

au3.note: When the end is still to come, Greek uses ἕως ἄν with the subjunctive after a primary verb, and ἕως with the optative after a secondary verb.

au4.note: Greek introduces an alternative question with πότερον and ἤ, or with εἰ and ἤ. After a primary tense the mood of the direct question remains, and after a secondary tense the optative may stand.
